Between 2 and 4 inches of snow fell from early morning to early afternoon on the 7th per observations between Portola and Susanville. From the afternoon of the 7th into the morning of the 8th, snow changed to freezing rain with between 0.1 and 0.5 inches of ice accumulation reported several miles to the west of Susanville.
Freezing rain resulted in 0.1 inches of ice 3 miles west-southwest of Gardnerville.

CALTRANS reported water from Long Valley Creek flowing over Highway 395. The highway was shut down in both directions starting around 1930PST on the 8th. In addition, County Road A26 (near Herlong) was closed due to weakened bridge supports. The end time is approximate and based on the end of heavier rain on the 9th. Damage from this specific event are unknown, although a preliminary damage assessment (CALTRANS) for flood repairs to Highway 395 in January and February totaled $1.8M.

The Secret Valley Rest area on Highway 395 was flooded, likely due to the overflow of a branch of Secret Creek. Highway 395 was closed between Wendel Road and Termo at around 2045PST on the 8th. The end time is approximate and based on the end of heavier rain on the 9th. Damages from this specific event are unknown, although a preliminary damage assessment (CALTRANS) for flood repairs to Highway 395 in January and February totaled $1.8M.

A large mudslide near the Donner Lake Interchange on Interstate 80 caused the closure of the freeway. The westbound lanes closed at 1802PST, followed by the eastbound lanes (downed power lines) at 1918PST. The road was completely closed between Kingvale and Truckee until 0520PST on the 9th when it was opened for local traffic and law enforcement. The freeway was fully opened at 1040PST on the 9th. The damage estimate was obtained from a preliminary damage assessment from CALTRANS.
The Middle Fork of the Feather River overflowed onto Highway 89 in Clio. The flooding caused a sinkhole in the road. The damage estimate is from a preliminary damage assessment from CALTRANS.
A bridge over Long Valley Creek in Lockwood was washed out after about 18 hours of moderate to heavy rain. The cost to repair the bridge is roughly estimated.
Six Mile Canyon Road was closed due to washouts and heavy damage. The cost to repair the damage is an estimate by the Storey County Public Works Director via a KTVN news article from April.

Highway 446 was destroyed by flood waters in more than 10 places on the southwest side of Pyramid Lake. Some sections were left with nearly 50-foot deep ravines. The highway was not re-opened to the public until early March. Repair cost based on Nevada Department of Transportation estimates from Reno-Gazette Journal article in February.

Twenty five structures, including at least 10 homes (one 8-plex and two single-family homes), were damaged by flood waters in Dayton by the morning of the 9th. Flooding of the two single family homes in East Dayton may have been largely due to breaks in ditches and culverts incapable of handling the exceptionally large volume of water. Water depth varied from 6 inches to as much as 3 feet on the south side of the Carson River. Standing flood waters lasted for at least several days after the initial flood surge on the 8th. Schools were closed county-wide on the 9th. The damage estimate from the Lyon County Emergency Manager is considered very low-end and could actually be several million dollars for Dayton alone.  In February, a Federal Disaster Declaration was approved for the January flooding.

Flooding from Steamboat Creek and the North Truckee Drain (near I-80 in Sparks) combined with some input from the Truckee River to bring a large area of lowland flooding between McCarran Blvd and Hidden Valley, as well as south of Interstate 80 in the Sparks Industrial area. Several days of notice allowed many businesses and homes in Hidden Valley (near Boynton Slough) to prepare flood mitigation measures including sandbagging. However, several homes in Hidden Valley still had flood damage due to overtopped sandbags and/or basement flooding.  The timing of the flood is approximate and the damage is roughly estimated.

Around 1300-1400 homes were evacuated in the Quilici area of South Reno due to flooding, likely from the overwhelming of Steamboat Ditch and nearby channels with the exceptionally heavy rainfall. The end timing of the flooding is roughly estimated. NOTE: No information is available regarding damage to homes.

Kingsbury Grade (Highway 207) was closed due to a previously-repaired (in December 2016) sinkhole re-opening with the heavy rain. The damage estimate is based on the contracts awarded for repairing both the December and January incidents.

The lowest lying areas of the Sierra Valley near the Middle Fork of the Feather River were inundated due to heavy rain runoff. As the valley drains very slowly, flooding of low-lying areas continued for an extended period of time with additional flooding in February. NOTE: no damage estimates were available.

Snowfall totals between the 9th and 12th were quite significant. Between the 9th and 12th, 6 to 10 feet of snow fell at ski areas near the Sierra crest, with 3 to 3.5 feet in the Tahoe City and Truckee areas, and 2 to 3 feet in the South Lake Tahoe area. During the evening of the 12th, two trees fell on three cars on CA route 89 near Squaw Valley, resulting in one death. A tree fell into a home in Kings Beach on the 11th, resulting in major damage. Numerous power outages were noted.

Between 6 and 9 feet of snow fell between the 9th and 12th in the the higher elevation of the northern Carson Range, including the Mount Rose and Diamond Peak ski areas. Farther south, Daggett Pass reported 45 inches of snowfall. Near lake level on the east side of Lake Tahoe, snowfall amounts ranged from 20 to 32 inches. Numerous power outages were noted and Incline Village declared a snow emergency with roads not expected to be cleared for at least a couple days.

SNOTEL-estimated snowfall totals of 3 to 5 feet fell between the 9th and 12th in the high Sierra and Sweetwater Range, with 4 to 5 inches of water equivalent (SWE) for several SNOTEL sites. At the high end, the Leavitt Lake SNOTEL recorded 10 inches of SWE, with 12 inches at the Mammoth Mountain ski area. Snowfall of 83 inches was measured at the Mammoth Mountain Ski area. Along and east of Highway 395, snowfall totals ranged from 12 to 20 inches.

The Portola cooperative observer reported 34 inches of snowfall from the 9th through the 12th. A CoCoRAHS site 5 miles west-northwest of Susanville reported 24 inches on the 9th before snow changed to rain (at about midnight on the 10th). Rain or a rain/snow mix changed back to all snow in lower elevations by the evening of the 11th. The Grizzly Ridge HADS at 6900 feet likely received at least 4 or 5 feet of snowfall based on sub-freezing temperatures and precipitation amounts near 8 inches.

All major travel routes through the Tahoe Basin were shut down for more than 24 hours due to poor visibility. Interstate 80 was closed at 2256PST on the 9th due to zero visibility, with the closure lasting through 1300PST on the 11th. With heavy snow and blizzard conditions moving over the rest of the area by early afternoon on the 10th, CA route 267 (Brockway Summit) was closed around 1300PST. Highway 50 was also shut down.

Several avalanches were reported in an avalanche-prone area of Alpine Meadows, with 12 to 14 homes affected (minor damage). One controlled avalanche hit at least several houses. A NWS meteorologist who lives in the area noted that a couple homes had damage to their garage doors due to the weight of the snow.

Highway 395 was shut down through all of Mono County for low visibility/blizzard conditions. Winds were gusting to between 35 and 58 mph in some spots along Highway 395 during the snowfall event, including near Bridgeport and the Mammoth airport.
Nevada route 341 (Mount Rose Highway) was closed for blizzard conditions into the morning of the 11th. Wind gusts at a couple RAWS sites were gusting between 35 and 45 mph during the snowfall event.

Virginia City received a total of 26 inches of snowfall (in multiple precipitation waves). Lower elevations received much less snowfall with periods of rain and snow. Elevations below 5500 feet mainly received between 2 and 4 inches of snowfall, although higher amounts to between 5 and 6.5 inches were noted in Sparks and north of Interstate 80 above 5000 feet.

Many locations from Yerington to Fernley to Fallon received between 1 and 3 inches of snowfall. However, a few sites between Fernley and Fallon reported between 5 and 6 inches of snowfall, mainly between early morning and mid afternoon on the 12th.
Wind gust measured at the Surprise Valley RAWS between 1130PST and 1230PST.

Sustained winds were as high as 63 mph at the Walker Lake NDOT sensor. Gusts at that site were mostly between 70 and 85 mph, but reached 105 mph at 1800PST. Smith Valley and Yerington has automated sensors with gusts briefly between 58 and 63 mph. The winds caused at least two semi-trucks to blow over on Highway 95 near Walker Lake.

Cooperative observers and CoCoRAHS observations around Lake Tahoe reported from just over 2 feet, to as much as 4.5 feet of snowfall between the 19th and early on the 23rd. At ski areas, an estimated 5 to 7 feet of snow fell. The weight of the snow caused the collapse of a building's roof in the Pioneer Center in South Lake Tahoe early in the morning on the 23rd.

A Facebook post with photos from the California Highway Patrol indicated an avalanche across Highway 89 between Alpine Meadows and Tahoe City. The avalanche was 200 feet across and 12 feet deep at the termination point near Highway 89. Two cars were buried; however, all occupants were rescued safely with no injuries.

The Portola cooperative observer measured 18 inches of snowfall in two precipitation waves between the evening of the 19th and very early on the 23rd. Two to 3 feet of snowfall is estimated to have fallen at higher elevations south and southwest of Susanville. Considerably less snow fell in the Susanville area, with between 3 and 8 inches reported, mostly falling between the evening of the 21st and 22nd.

Mammoth Mountain ski area reported between 6 and 7 feet of snowfall between the 20th and 23rd. Elsewhere in the higher elevations, an estimated 4 to 6 feet of snow fell at SNOTEL sites near the crest, with 2 to 3 feet east of Highway 395. Fourteen to 20 inches of snow fell at cooperative observer and CoCoRAHS sites near Highway 395, with the heaviest accumulations on the 22nd into the 23rd.  On January 30, a local state of emergency was declared for Mammoth Lakes due to storm damages and the cost of snow removal since early in the month.
Cooperative observers reported between 2 and 3 feet of snow on the east shore of Lake Tahoe and for the Daggett Pass area. The Mount Rose ski area reported more than 6 feet of snow.

Widespread snowfall totals of 4 to 8 inches were noted in valley locations through the evening of the 22nd, mainly near and west of Interstate 580/Highway 395, with lesser amounts of 2 to 4 inches farther east. Local amounts between 8 and 13 inches were reported in the foothills west and southwest of Reno. Finally, between the 20th and 23rd, Virginia City received almost 27 inches of snow.
A trained weather spotter located 8 miles south of Reno reported a 56 knot (65 mph) wind gust.
A trained weather spotter located 5 miles WSW of Gardnerville reported a 53 knot (61 mph) wind gust.  The strong wind blew an antenna off of his roof.
A 50 knot (58 mph) wind gust was recorded by the Black Springs NDOT station in Golden Valley 7 miles north of Reno.
A 55 knot (63 mph) wind gust was recorded at the Washoe Valley NDOT station 3 miles south of Washoe City.  Blowing snow was reducing visibility to less than 1/4 mile at times.
The Nevada Highway Patrol reported that an empty tractor-trailer was blown over by strong winds on U.S. Highway 395 near the Red Rock exit 10 miles northwest of Reno.
The Reno Gazette-Journal reported that two power lines were down and arcing on Moana Lane, forcing the rerouting of traffic.  Approximately 600 customers in the area were without power.
An off-duty NWS employee located in southwest Reno reported a 65 knot (75 mph) wind gust at an elevation of 4880 feet.
A 56 knot (65 mph) wind gust was recorded at the National Weather Service Forecast Office in north Reno.
A 54 knot (62 mph) wind gust was recorded by the wind sensor at Wolf Run Golf Course in south Reno.

Major flooding from the Pit River affected much of Big Valley between the 7th and 14th. The Reno National Weather Service hydrologist toured the area for picture evidence.||NOTE: There was clearly damage to some homes and structures in the Bieber area as evidenced by pictures; however, no storm damage estimates were available to the Storm Data preparer.

The Middle Fork of the Feather River saw record flooding (a record crest at Portola on the 10th) and caused extensive structural damage in Portola, Clio, and downstream to Blairsden. Highway 89 was closed near Clio due to water over the road. Many schools were closed on the 9th in the Portola area and along the Feather River. Damage estimate only for repairs to Highway 89 (per a CALTRANS report) so actual flooding damage likely much higher.

Major flooding on the Susan River caused extensive damage in and to the east of Susanville from the afternoon of the 9th into the 10th. The flooding prompted the evacuation of a number of homes and apartment complexes in Susanville during the afternoon and evening of the 9th. The damage estimate for this event is rough and could be significantly in error.

Flooding from creeks covered the intersection of Highways 49 and 89 in Sierraville on the afternoon of the 9th.  Shallow water was photographed up against buildings at the Sierraville Ranger Station on the morning of the 10th. A washout caused the closure of Highway 49 between Sattley and Yuba Pass. Damage estimates are only for repairs to Highways 49 and 89 based on a CALTRANS report.

Heavy rain fell in areas with significant snow berms and blocked storm drains, resulting in substantial flooding to around 50 homes in the Meyers area. Some of the worst flood damage was seen on Nahane Dr and Wailaki St per a KCRA news article. The end time of the flooding is estimated. Damage estimates are also roughly estimated.

Heavy rain combined with snow berms and clogged storm drains to bring flooding to around 10 homes in South Lake Tahoe starting on the 8th. Bill and Shirley Avenues saw the most flooding damage per a KCRA news article. The damages are roughly estimated.

Twelve to 16 inches of water was running over Mt Rose Highway in the Tahoe Meadows area (near the highway summit) on the morning of the 8th. The highway was closed between Incline Village and the summit until the afternoon of the 9th due to the flooding.

County officials noted that 13 homes were threatened by waters overflowing from Swan Lake and nearby ditches on the 10th. Flooding continued through May, with the worst threat in March as additional rainfall and snowmelt input from Peavine Peak exacerbated flooding. Significant flooding continued into April before mitigation efforts began to contain the flooding.

Widespread gusts between 60 and 70 mph were recorded in the valleys on the 9th, with gusts 70 to as high as 92 mph (Browns Creek Bridge on I-580) in the foothills. Numerous downed trees and power lines were noted, with as many as 7,000 to 8,000 customers without power early in the afternoon, mostly in Douglas County. A big rig was blown over on Highway 395 near Stead. Finally, at least 7 flights into the Reno-Tahoe International airport were delayed or cancelled due to the winds.

Wind gusts between 60 and 82 mph were recorded along Highway 395 between Bridgeport and Crowley Lake on the 9th. According to the California Highway Patrol, two semi-trucks were blown over in Lee Vining with another blown over near the Mammoth airport.
The Reno-Tahoe International airport recorded a gust to 73 mph at 1934PST on the 6th. Gusts 65 to 73 mph were noted in the foothills along Interstate 580 south of Reno and near the Stead airport.
The Surprise Valley RAWS recorded gusts between 61 and 71 mph on the 9th.

High winds were noted along Highway 395 south of Janesville. Winds were sustained over 40 mph at the Doyle CALTRANS site, with gusts to 63 mph at the Doyle RAWS. A semi-truck was blown over near Hallelujah Junction.

Winds over Sweetwater Summit (NV Highway 338) were sustained between 45 and 62 mph with gusts up to 82 mph on the 9th. Elsewhere, Wellington recorded gusts up to 59 mph and the Walker Lake NDOT had brief periods of high winds with gusts as high as 76 mph.

Periodic sustained winds over 40 mph with gusts as high as 62 mph were reported in various locations from near Lovelock (Toulon NDOT site) south and west to near Lahontan Reservoir (Bango DRI site) and Fallon (Naval Air Station).

Between 2 and 4 feet of snow fell at ski areas on the 9th and 10th. Below 7000 feet, snow amounts fell off substantially as significant amounts of rain fell there. At 6300 and 6700 feet in Incline Village 10 and 18 inches was reported, respectively. In Tahoe City near lake level, only 7 inches was reported by a cooperative observer. In South Lake Tahoe, only 3 inches fell at the airport.

For elevations above 8500 feet, 2 to 3 feet of snow fell near the Sierra crest with around 18 inches east of Highway 395 and north of Bridgeport. At 8200 feet in Mammoth Lakes, 16 inches was reported by a National Weather Service spotter. Below 7500 feet along Highway 395, mostly rain fell with snowfall totals only reaching 1 to 2 inches.
Wind gusts in the foothills of far western Nevada and in the north valleys of Reno ranged from 60 to 75 mph on the 16th.
Sustained winds between 40 and 50 mph with gusts 60 to 84 mph occurred over Sweetwater Summit and along Highway 95 near Walker Lake on the morning of the 16th.

Four to 5 feet of snow was reported at ski areas from the 20th to the 22nd. Between 22 and 34 inches of snow was reported near lake level on the north and west sides of Lake Tahoe, with 15 to 17 inches near South Lake Tahoe. Interstate 80 was periodically closed due to spinouts and low visibility, with the longest full closure between 1422PST and 2129PST on the 21st.

Seven to 11 inches of snow fell in valleys from Susanville south and west to Portola and Sierraville, mainly from the evening of the 21st to the morning of the 22nd. In the higher elevations, an estimated 22 inches of snow fell at the Independence Creek SNOTEL, with at least 4 feet likely at the Grizzle Ridge HADS (around 7.5 inches of liquid equivalent precipitation).
Six inches fell at the Cedarville Cooperative Observer station.

An estimated 3 to 4 feet of snow fell near the Sierra crest between the 20th and 22nd, with around 2 feet for high elevations east of Highway 395 (Lobdell Lake SNOTEL). Cooperative observers along Highway 395 received minimal snowfall (up to 2 inches) as snow levels remained elevated until early on the 22nd.

Around 5 feet of snow fell at ski areas in the Carson Range, with 3 feet at Daggett Pass, between the 20th and 22nd. In Incline Village at 6700 feet, 40 inches of snow was noted by a spotter. Below 6500 feet, 12 to 22 inches of snowfall was reported by cooperative observers. Mount Rose Highway (NV 431) was closed due to a localized avalanche on the evening of the 20th.

Widespread snowfall totals of 5 to 10 inches were noted on the north and west sides of Reno, including Stead and Cold Springs Valley, with 16 inches in Virginia City. In the lower valleys around Reno-Sparks, 2 to 4 inches was reported including 3.7 inches at the Reno-Tahoe airport.
Four inches of snow was reported in Cedarville.

Ten to 20 inches of snowfall fell from just west of Susanville south and west to Portola and the Sierra Valley, including 16 inches in Portola and 11 inches 4 miles south-southwest of Susanville. Lesser amounts of 4 to 6 inches were noted along and east of Highway 395.
Between 2 and 3.5 feet of snow fell at ski areas west and south of Lake Tahoe, with 17 to 24 inches around Lake Tahoe and northeast to Boca Reservoir and near Verdi.

Fifteen to 19 inches of snow fell in the Carson Range and near Lake Tahoe, generally near and south of Highway 50. To the northeast of Lake Tahoe, 23 to 28 inches of snow was reported between Incline Village and the Mount Rose Ski area.

Isolated snowfall amounts between 17 and 19 inches fell above 5000 feet west of Carson City on the 5th, with around 12 inches in Virginia City. Four to six inches of snow fell on the north and west sides of Reno, as well as near Carson City and east of Highway 395 in the Minden-Johnson Lane area. Six to 8 inches of snow was reported in the north valleys of Reno. Lesser snowfall amounts up to 3 inches fell in Sparks and in southeast Reno.

Sustained winds between 30 and 50 mph, with gusts up to 75 mph, were recorded at the Walker Lake NDOT and Hawthorne airport. Highway 95 between Schurz and Hawthorne was closed at 0115PST on the 7th due to the high winds.

Seven to 13 inches of snow fell along Highway 70 between 3 miles east of Beckwourth and Portola, with 15 inches reported on social media in Lake Davis. Near Susanville, only 2 to 4.5 inches of snowfall was noted.

Two to 3 feet of snow fell at the June and Mammoth Mountain ski areas. Near Highway 395 north of Bridgeport (Devil's Gate Summit), 10 inches of snow was reported by the public, with only 2 to 3 inches noted by the Bridgeport and Lee Vining cooperative observers.
Wind gust measured at the Bull Flat RAWS. The time of the gust was estimated based on radar information.

The wind gust was measured at Lovelock-Derby Field. Visibility was reduced to 1.25 miles due to blowing dust with the outflow winds. Another thunderstorm brought visibility as low as 1/4 mile between 1810PST and 1820PST (with gusts up to 53 mph).
The wind gust was measured at Lovelock-Derby Field. The wind was generated by outflow from earlier thunderstorms.
The wind gust (from the south) was measured at the Minden-Tahoe airport.

Thunderstorms with heavy rainfall persisted for almost 2 hours in the hills east of Yerington (near the Lyon/Mineral County line). A deputy sheriff reported a large wall of water coming down from the hills (in a typically dry wash). A National Weather Service employee investigated the scene a week later and noticed high water marks as much as 2.5 feet above Prospect St, with water damage to landscaping for multiple properties. Appreciable sediment was noted on Bybee Ln, Almond Rd, and Prospect St, with damage to Bybee Ln. (unpaved road). Damage roughly estimated based on little or no known home damage (mainly landscaping, unpaved roads).

The Truckee Fire burned around 99,000 acres to the north and northeast of Fernley (and north of Interstate 80) between the 3rd and 10th. Extreme fire growth in grass and brush lead to the voluntary evacuation of 10 to 12 homes on Duffy Road northeast of Fernley on the 3rd; however, no homes were destroyed or damaged as fire fighters set up successful protection lines. Interstate 80 was closed between the evening of the 3rd and early morning on the 4th. The cost to fight the fire was in excess of $600K.

The Earthstone Fire burned over 41,000 acres (mainly north of Interstate 80) as periods of extreme fire behavior allowed it to spread between the hills east of Sparks to several miles west of Wadsworth. Interstate 80 was closed, mainly between mile markers 22 and 43 from the evening of the 3rd into early morning on the 4th. The fire was suspected to be human-caused with no lightning or downed power lines in the area. The cost to fight the fire totaled at least $3.5M.

The Winnemucca Ranch Fire east of Pyramid Highway and in Palomino Valley burned around 4800 acres. Although 58 structures were threatened at the onset of the fire, the fire only wound up destroying one mobile home and two outbuildings on Amy Road. The fire was human-caused.

The Farad Fire burned 747 acres in the steep terrain on the north and west side of Interstate 80 about 1 mile west of the California-Nevada state line, mostly on the 10th and 11th. The incident caused periodic closures of Interstate 80 on the 10th into the afternoon of the 11th due to fire fighting activities. A few power poles were damaged near Interstate 80. As the burn was in steep terrain with narrow canyons, it likely contributed to mudslides and debris flows which affected Interstate 80 in August.
A mud and debris flow caused the closure of the Ramsey Weeks Cutoff between Highway 50 and Alternate US 50 on the afternoon of the 24th.

Eighteen power poles were snapped along Farm District Road, with short dry grass completely stripped from a nearby field. The wind gust was an estimate based on a utility company foreman's experience, who stated that it usually takes around 100 mph to snap power poles cleanly. Minor damage was reported to 4 homes and numerous billboards along Interstate 80 near mile marker 48, with moderate damage to 3 trucks and 2 outbuildings. Radar and damage patterns (examined by a NWS employee) did not indicate any rotation so straight-line winds are the most probable cause.

A funnel cloud was photographed in the Gabbs Valley Range east of Hawthorne, with the position an estimate based on observed terrain features. It is possible that there was a tornado touchdown; however, terrain obscured the base of the funnel and no additional evidence was available.

A nearly stationary thunderstorm west-southwest of Pyramid Lake produced 1.25 inches of rain in less than an hour. The USGS stream gauge on Hardscrabble Creek registered a 5-foot rise in its level in about 40 minutes from 1515���1555PST. Nevada Department of Transporation reported debris and rocks on Nevada Highway 445 just south of Sutcliffe, Nevada, with all lanes blocked. No damage estimates were available.

A nearly stationary thunderstorm produced over 2 inches of rain and caused a debris flow across Nevada Highway 447 south of Gerlach, Nevada. Nevada Department of Transportation reported mud and debris in the roadway blocking all lanes in both directions. No damage estimates were available.

A pulse thunderstorm produced a strong outflow that caused 3-foot whitecaps along Washoe Lake along with several snapped tree limbs 3���4 inches in diameter. Washoe Valley Mesonet reported a 59 MPH wind gust from 1625���1630PST.
Reports of hail between 1500���1530PST in downtown Susanville with the largest hail up to golf ball size occurring closer to 1530PST. Leaves removed from many trees and garden plants damaged.
A pulse thunderstorm produced a 53-knot peak gust at the Hot Springs Mountain HADS site.

A training thunderstorm caused flash flooding and a debris flow on the westbound side of Interstate-80 near Farad, CA, which closed the interstate from approximately 1745���1920PST. This area was associated with steep terrain and the burn scar from the Farad Fire. No damage estimates were available.
A severe thunderstorm near Emerald Bay/D. L. Bliss State Park dropped large hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter. No damage estimates/reports were available.
An area of pulse thunderstorms caused boulders to slide onto Nevada State Highway 28 at mile marker 3. No damage reports/estimates were available.

Nevada Department of Transportation reported water over roadway along Interstate-580 and Damonte Ranch Parkway from a line of thunderstorms. Multiple vehicle accidents were reported, however, no estimate of damages were reported.

The Slinkard Fire burned 8,925 acres west of Topaz, California, between August 29th and September 11th. The fire was suspected to be lightning-caused by a high-based thunderstorm. Extreme fire growth in cheat grass, sagebrush, and pinyon/juniper lead to evacuations in Topaz north of California 89 to the Nevada state line. U.S. 395 was closed from south of Gardnerville, Nevada, to California 108 in Bridgeport, California, from August 31st to September 2nd. California 89 was also closed from U.S. 395 to State Road 4 at Monitor Pass. Nevada 208 was also closed for a short period of time. The cost to fight the fire was at least $5.7M.

The Tohakum 2 Fire burned 94,221 acres approximately 40 miles north of Nixon, Nevada, between August 29th and September 12th. No structures were lost, but power lines were damaged and traffic on Nevada 447 was affected by flames and smoke for several days, making travel difficult for Burning Man attendees headed to the Black Rock Desert. The fire was suspected to be started by a lightning strike from a high-based thunderstorm. The cost to fight the fire was at least $3.5M.

The Tohakum 2 Fire burned 94,221 acres approximately 40 miles north of Nixon, Nevada, between August 29th and September 12th. No exact end time was found for this incident. No structures were lost, but power lines were damaged and traffic on Nevada 447 was affected by flames and smoke for several days, making travel difficult for Burning Man attendees headed to the Black Rock Desert. The fire was suspected to be started by a lightning strike from a high-based thunderstorm. The cost to fight the fire was at least $3.5M.

An outflow from a line of thunderstorms produced a 57-knot peak gust at the KRNO ASOS. Airport observers also noted that visibility dropped to 3 statute miles south of the northward-moving gust front.
A strong thunderstorm located near Lovelock Airport produced a wind gust of 59 knots.
Ranger at DL Bliss State Park reported quarter size hail accumulating up to a half inch on ground.
Public reported nickel size hail via Facebook.

North Lake Tahoe Fire Protection District reported a confirmed tornado/waterspout a mile off the northeastern shore of Lake Tahoe near Sand Harbor, Nevada. The position of the tornado was estimated based on a video and terrain features. Numerous other spotter photos also showed a well-defined spray ring on the water surface of Lake Tahoe. The tornado was determined to be an EF-0 as no damage was reported. This tornado was associated with a supercell thunderstorm.

United States Forest Service employee reported a confirmed funnel cloud near the Rafter 7 Ranch. The funnel cloud was also photographed by Nevada Creeks and Communities at an event at Rafter 7 Ranch. The position was estimated based on the observation from the USFS employee.

A citizen reported a confirmed tornado/waterspout that formed two brief spin-ups on Lake Tahoe near Cave Rock, Nevada. The position of the tornado was estimated based on pictures and terrain features. The tornado was determined to be an EF-0 as no damage was reported. This tornado was non-supercellular in nature.

A dry slab avalanche occurred on Tamarack Peak within the Hourglass Bowl at 0900PST 16 November and partially buried a female skier and totally buried a male skier. A quote from the Sierra Avalanche Center: The person who was still skiing when the avalanche hit her was blown out of her skis and they were buried. She may have hit a tree and her back began seizing up. The person buried had both skis but lost a pole and one skin and had a torn ligament in his ankle. Therefore from this report, it is evident that both the skiers were injured in this avalanche.

Public reported that a tree limb fell onto a second story balcony landing on Patriot Drive in southeast Reno the morning of 20 December. Wind gust readings from a nearby mesonet (IEINV) had shown maximum wind gusts in the previous 12 hours as high as 62 mph (20 December 0118PST).

Light snow occurred the morning and afternoon of 22 February. A crash was reported on Interstate 80 eastbound near the Mustang exit involving approximately 20 vehicles at approximately 1400PST 22 February according to Nevada Highway Patrol. Interstate 80 was closed from 1400PST to 1700PST 22 February. The Reno Gazette Journal reported 8 injuries from this crash. Nevada Highway Patrol reported that no cause was determined at the time of the accident.

A multi-car crash occurred the afternoon of the 22nd involving as many as 35 cars south of Reno near the Galena Creek Bridge on Interstate 580 according to the Nevada Highway Patrol. Northbound Interstate 580 was closed at the bridge from approximately 1647 PST to 1945 PST 22 February. According to the Nevada Highway Patrol, the cause was likely ice on the road from light snowfall.

California Highway Patrol stated that a GMC pickup driven by a male was heading south on US 395 near Green Creek Road when it lost control on the snow covered roadway and overturned into Virginia Creek. Authorities say both passengers were able to get out of the truck as it started to fill up with water. Fire crews cut the driver out of the truck, where he was transported to Mammoth Lakes Hospital by Mono County Paramedics. He was pronounced deceased at the hospital at approximately 0905PST 23 February. Troopers stated that icy roads may be to blame. Source of the report: Reno KTVN 2 News.

Interstate 80 closed from Colfax, CA, to the Nevada State line due to high winds, heavy snowfall, and whiteout conditions. The closure of Interstate 80 lasted from the early afternoon of 1 March through the late morning of 2 March. Chain and snow tires were required on several roads around the Greater Lake Tahoe Area. A snowboarder became lost during the blizzard conditions the night of the 1st and was found deceased near Squaw Valley Ski Resort 2 March at 1017PST. The cause of death from several reports is undetermined. Wind gusts during peak blizzard conditions ranged from 47 to 63 mph in the Greater Lake Tahoe area below 8,000 feet MSL, with the highest wind gust of 146 mph reported at 1 March 2134PST from a mesonet atop the summit of Squaw Valley.

A collapsing core within a thunderstorm produced heavy rainfall over the Slinkard burn scar west of Topaz Lake, which caused two pronounced debris flows off the burn scar onto U.S. Highway 395 near the California/Nevada state line. The debris flows were up to 5 feet deep in a few places and closed the highway for over 18 hours while crews removed the flow. Nearly 200 people from the nearby Topaz Lodge were forced to the second floor as mud hit the exterior part of the first floor. No injuries were reported. No damage estimates were available from Topaz Lodge. The portable RAWS site above the Slinkard Fire burn scar (NCRC1; elevation 7451 feet) recorded 0.27 inches of rainfall in 15 minutes at the time two debris flows were reported (21 May 1727PST). A total of 0.90 inches of rainfall eventually fell on the burn scar in a two and a half hour time period from 21 May 1652PST to 1922PST. The cost to clear the debris flow for the Nevada Department of Transportation was a total of $51,476, which includes labor and equipment costs.

A person living one mile southeast of Eagleville reported very strong winds the morning of February 7th.  This person's home weather station recorded wind gusts of 65 to over 90 mph.  The strongest gust was reported to be 105 mph.  Localized damage occurred in the area.  A barbeque grill was picked up by the wind and thrown through a glass sunroom.  A 500-gallon diesel fuel tank was blown off of its pedestal.  Shingles were peeled from roofs and branches were broken off trees.

According to the Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center, a full course slab avalanche was accidentally triggered on a 40 degree slope by two snow travelers who were utilizing splitboards to travel in the Ripper Chute on the Dana Plateau at an elevation of 11600 feet MSL (above treeline on the northeast aspect of Mount Dana) at approximately 23 March 1030PST. One snow traveler was able to self-arrest, while the climber 10 feet below was swept the entire course of the couloir. The lower climber sustained minor injuries and was able to walk/glissade on a shovel out to the trailhead. Technical details of the avalanche were as follows. The weak layer was storm snow. The bed surface was old snow. The crown height of the avalanche was 2 feet. The avalanche average length and width were 1000 feet and 20 feet, respectively. The avalanche was estimated to be a D2 in destructive size (could bury, injure, or kill a person) and an R3 in relative size (medium, relative to the path). According to the report, there was precipitation in the form of snow with less than a 1 in per hour accumulation rate. Overcast skies, bad visibility, and blowing snow with strong southeast winds were also observed.

The Jasper Fire in northern Sun Valley burned 1,165 acres from 13 July 1400PST to 16 July 1700PST. Sierra Front Dispatch Center stated that one home and two outbuildings were destroyed. At one point more than 100 homes were threatened, and the Washoe County Sheriff���s Office was going door-to-door urging people to evacuate. Firefighting costs were approximately $769K USD according to the Nevada Bureau of Land Management.

A 9-year-old Reno girl died on 19 July from injuries she suffered when strong winds blew an inflatable bounce house with three children inside into power lines.  The Washoe County Sheriff's Office says the bounce house was uplifted about 10 feet and got caught on the lines in a south Reno neighborhood. Deputies and firefighters rescued the children. They treated two for minor injuries at the scene and transported the 9-year-old girl to the hospital, where she succumbed to her injuries 19 July. The incident occurred on the afternoon of 14 July around 1500PST. Authorities told KOLO-TV the bounce house seemed to be secured to the ground but was caught by an especially strong gust of wind. Winds were sustained 15-20 mph with gusts 20-25 mph at nearby Reno-Tahoe International Airport around the incident time.

Strong outflow winds from nearby decaying thunderstorms blew a small tree down, blew the siding of a single-wide trailer off, blew metal roofing panels off another single-wide trailer, and damaged a metal overhang on a flat-roofed store. Wind gusts were estimated to be 50-55 mph. The damage was estimated based upon the costs of the materials damaged.

The Long Valley Fire started near the Red Rock exit along US Highway 395 and spread across the California/Nevada border into northwestern Nevada the 24th before being contained the 27th. The fire burned 2438 acres, and one structure was destroyed. The Federal Emergency Management Agency stated that the fire threatened 250-300 homes in and around Rancho Haven (Nevada). The fire also threatened five buildings, infrastructure, utilities, equipment, farms, ranches, and a watershed in the area. Mandatory evacuations were ordered for approximately 800 people before containment was reached. Firefighting costs were approximately $600K, according to the Nevada Bureau of Land Management.

The Walker Fire burned in Genesee Valley in the Plumas National Forest east of Taylorsville from the afternoon of the 4th through the 25th. Smoke from this fire affected parts of western Nevada and northeast California, with the most widespread smoke reaching the Reno Metropolitan area on the 8th. This fire would eventually burn 54,612 acres before heavy rain on the 16th ended nearly all remaining fire activity, with full containment achieved on the 25th. Several evacuations were ordered for the Genesee Valley corridor, the Ward Creek area, the Flournoy Bridge area, and Antelope Lake. According to the Plumas National Forest, 9 structures were destroyed in the fire and the cost was estimated to be near $35,100,000.

A large avalanche occurred between the Scott Chute and the Promised Land at Alpine Meadows Resort. 2 individuals were involved with one fatal injury with the other skier having severe lower-body injuries. A strong winter storm had hit in the previous 12-24 hours with 25 inches at the summit and over 15 inches at the base. Weather was mostly cloudy with high clouds at the time of the avalanche and light winds.

The Sierra Avalanche Center reported a full burial slab avalanche along the north side of Independence Lake. One skier of three triggered the slab avalanche about 40 feet from the crown line. The crown size varied from 10 to 48 inches and went about 100 feet wide. The slide went from an elevation of about 8400 feet MSL down to 7400 feet MSL. The skier tried to ski out at a fast 45 degrees to the left but was immediately buried. This person was buried for a total of 45 minutes. The skier's only injuries were some bruising and a small cut. The two other skiers were left unscathed about 200 feet from the bottom edge of the avalanche.

A mesoanticyclone embedded within a deep pyrocumulonimbus updraft inside the Loyalton wildfire perimeter generated an EF1 rated anticyclonic tornado that snapped (DI 28, DOD 4) and uprooted (DI 28, DOD 3) several Jeffrey pine trees along a 0.43-mile path within Roberts Canyon. The tornado spun up 0.15 miles north-northeast of the intersection of Forest Service Road 182 and Forest Service Road 31182 and dissipated 0.44 miles east of the aforementioned intersection. The damage path had a maximum width of 137 yards. No injuries or deaths occurred with this tornado.

A mesoanticyclone embedded within a deep pyrocumulonimbus updraft inside the Loyalton wildfire perimeter generated an EF1 rated anticyclonic tornado that snapped several quaking aspen trees (DI 27, DOD 4) along a 0.09-mile path on the northeast facing slope of Roberts Canyon. The tornado spun up 0.37 miles south-southwest of the intersection of Forest Service Road 182 and Forest Service Road 31182 and dissipated 0.46 miles south-southwest of the aforementioned intersection. The damage path had a maximum width of 20 yards. No injuries or deaths occurred with this tornado.

Bystanders along CA 70 and US 395 near Hallelujah Junction captured multiple videos and photographs of an anticyclonically rotating tornado pendant to the base of a pyrocumulonimbus cloud. The tornado caused no damage from which the NWS could assign an EF-scale rating as it traversed across an area of burned sagebrush. From photographs and video evidence, the approximate path of the tornado was calculated. The tornado traveled along a 3.16-mile path from the head of Roberts Canyon to 1.33 miles southwest of Hallelujah Junction. The maximum path width was approximately 156 yards. No injuries or deaths occurred with this tornado.

A 47-year-old Nevada man died after being struck by lightning while on a jet ski at Stampede Reservoir in Sierra County on Saturday 25 July. His body went underwater near the boat ramp and divers later found his body 20 yards from the shoreline. For the higher elevations of western Nevada, snowfall around the Carson Range and the Lake Tahoe Basin was generally around 4 to 10 inches above 7000 feet MSL. Near Incline Village, 2 inches of snow fell.

Widespread high winds impacted the Eastern Sierra and Mono County in the pre-dawn hours of February 3. 109 MPH at Lundy RAWS and 83 MPH at Mammoth Lakes Airport were notable observations. Even such, no significant damage was reported. High profile vehicle prohibitions were in effect on Highway 395.
NDOT weather station near Walker Lake hit 62 MPH.

For the higher elevations of western Nevada, snowfall around the northern portion of the Carson Range and the Lake Tahoe Basin was generally around 2 to 3 inches above 6500 feet MSL. Along the south and east shore, up to an inch fell.

Heavy snow impacted the Eastern Sierra with 18 inches reported at Mammoth Mountain summit with 15 inches at the snow study plot near 9000 feet, 8 inches at June Mountain, and 7 inches at Rock Creek.

Heavy snow affected the Lake Tahoe area with up to 16 inches at Alpine Ski, 10 inches at Tahoe Donner, 12 inches at Northstar, and 11 inches at Heavenly Ski. Elsewhere lower in elevation around 4 inches of snow fell near Truckee and South Lake Tahoe. Additional lighter snows persisted into the 13th with amounts generally 1-4 inches in mountain communities with up to 6-7 inches additional at the ski areas.
Diamond Peak Ski reported 9 inches with Mt Rose 7 inches. Additional light snow fell into the 13th with 6 inches additional at each location.
Gusts between 55-60 mph measured at NDOT site near Hawthorne and Walker Lake.
Numerous gusts 50-60 mph along the foothills in Northwest Reno, Caughlin Ranch, Washoe Valley, and west of Carson City.
Strong winds impacted the Eastern Sierra with gusts to 86 MPH on Mammoth Mountain. Wind gusts in the valleys and closer to Highway 395 were closer to 45-50 MPH. No appreciable impacts noted.
Light to moderate snowfall. Generally 3 to 8 inches around the Truckee Tahoe region.
Light snowfall around the Sierra Front. 1 to 3 inches reported.
Widespread gusts 50-60 MPH across the Sierra Front including 57 MPH near Minden and 55 near Spanish Springs. Mt Rose gusted to 80 MPH.

Strong winds around the Eastern Sierra with gusts 45-60 MPH along Highway 395 including 57 MPH near Conway Summit and 52 MPH near Lee Vining. Mammoth Mountain summit peaked at a relatively modest 69 MPH.

Numerous reports of high winds along Highway 395 in Mono County pre-dawn. 99 MPH at Lundy RAWS, 98 MPH from Liberty Utilities sensor near Topaz Lake, 95 MPH at Mammoth Mountain Summit, 75 MPH at Walker RAWS, 67 MPH at Mammoth Airport. Even with these strong winds no major impacts were noted except a high profile vehicle prohibition by Caltrans along Highway 395.
Gusts to 71 MPH noted at Tahoe Donner and 69 MPH at Rice Canyon.
Little Valley RAWS hit 80 MPH peak gust. 58 MPH at nearby Galena.

Numerous gusts above 55-60 MPH in the southern Sierra Front including 66 MPH at NV Energy station near Genoa and 58 MPH at Holbrook Junction. Over 3000 customers without power in the Minden and Gardnerville areas.
Gust to 73 mph at NDOT Sweetwater Summit station.
Light snow amounts of 2 to 4 inches in the Lake Tahoe basin and Truckee areas.

Snowfall of 1 to 4 inches across the Tahoe basin and Truckee.

Snowfall up to 3 inches on the east side of the Tahoe basin.

Snow showers brought 1 to 3 inches snowfall to Highway 395 communities in the eastern Sierra, with 4 inches at Bodie and 6 inches at Mammoth Mountain.
Snowfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches in the Truckee, Tahoe areas with higher amounts west of Highway 89 including 8 at Homewood Ski and Squaw Valley, and 6 at Tahoe Donner.

Variable snowfall on Tahoe east side with under an inch at lake level and 4 inches at Mt Rose Ski.
Light snow or rain/snow mix for Tahoe and Truckee. 1 to 4 inches new snowfall. Northstar Ski reported 7 inches new snow.

Periods of heavy rain, with a rain/snow mix at times. 0.88 inches of rainfall.

Widespread gusts of 45-57 mph in the Sierra Valley and along the US 395 corridor between Susanville and the California-Nevada state line. A peak wind gust of 58 mph was measured by the LIB24 mesonet 3 miles southeast of Dog Valley.

Widespread high winds impacted the Eastern Sierra and Mono County during the morning and afternoon of January 4. 108 MPH at Mammoth Mountain and 79 MPH at Conway Summit were notable observations. June Lake Fire Department reported multiple 2-foot diameter trees blown down or snapped in high winds.

Light to moderate snow affected the Lake Tahoe region with up to 12 inches at Squaw Valley Ski, 8 inches at Homewood Ski, 6 inches at Northstar Ski, 5 inches at Independence Lake, 3 inches at Heavenly Ski, and 2 inches at Tahoe Donner Ski.
Light snow fell at Mammoth Mountain Ski the 4th into the early morning hours of the 5th with 4 inches measured at the base of the resort.

Gusty south-southwest winds mainly 40 to 55 mph were felt along the lower valleys of the Basin and Range of western Nevada. The highest measured wind gusts were 60 MPH and 59 MPH along the Black Rock Desert and near Toulon, respectively.
Gusts between 59-62 MPH were measured at NDOT sites near Schurz and Walker Lake.

Strong southwest winds impacted western Nevada with widespread gusts 40 to 55 mph felt across many lower valleys. Wind gusts greater than 58 mph were seen in western Reno, Washoe Valley, southwestern Carson City, along US-50 between Dayton and Silver Springs, and along US-395 in the Carson Valley. The highest wind gust was measured atop Peavine Mountain with a reading of 103 mph. Nevada Highway Patrol reported that a 53-foot box trailer was pushed over by the strong winds near Minden during the early afternoon of the 4th. Minor injuries were reported.

Strong southwest winds impacted the eastern portion of the Lake Tahoe Basin and the Carson Range with several wind gusts 40 to 55 mph measured. Wind gusts up to 48 to 54 mph were measured along the surface of Lake Tahoe. Rough lake conditions were noted.

Widespread gusts of 40-55 mph were seen across much of the Greater Lake Tahoe Area. Wind gusts up to 54 mph were seen along the surface of Lake Tahoe. A peak wind gust of 136 mph was measured by the Siberia mesonet atop Squaw Valley.
Light to moderate snow affected the Lake Tahoe region with up to 8 inches at Mount Rose Ski, 4 inches at the Big Meadows SNOTEL, and 1 inch of snow at Diamond Peak Ski.

Ridgetop wind gusts along the western portion of the Lake Tahoe Basin were as high as 124 to 137 mph at Squaw Valley Siberia and Ward Mountain, respectively. Below ridgetops, winds gusted mainly 35 to 50 mph, with the surface of Lake Tahoe seeing gusts 42 to 54 mph. The main impacts were shut down ski lifts and choppy lake conditions.
The Washoe 204-Farad LIB15 mesonet reported several northerly wind gusts between 35 to 50 mph with a couple stand out 59 mph gusts during the morning of the 19th.
The upper ridgetops of Mammoth Mountain Ski Area saw wind gusts as high as 117 to 119 mph from the 18th into the 19th. Lower down on the mountain gusts as high as 62 mph were seen.

The mid-to-upper elevations of the northern Carson Range experienced north and easterly wind gusts from 45 to 79 mph. The 79 mph gust occurred atop Slide Mountain. At the surface of Lake Tahoe, winds gusted from 42 to 54 mph with areas along the eastern shore experiencing gusts 35 to 45 mph.

From the 22nd into the early part of the 23rd, light accumulating snowfall up to an inch occurred along the CA 139 and US 395 corridor from Spaulding south to Doyle. Two miles south-southeast of Dog Valley, 2.5 inches of snow fell.

Around the Lake Tahoe Basin, 3 to 5 inches of snow fell at Homewood Ski, 2 inches fell at Heavenly Ski, 1.5 inches fell near Boca Reservoir, 1 inch fell near Northstar Ski Area, and 1 inch fell at Tahoe City. No large impacts were noted.
At Mammoth Mountain Ski, 2 to 3 inches of snow fell.
Light snowfall accumulations of 1 to 2 inches were noted along the northern portion of the Carson Range from Mount Rose Ski to Diamond Peak Ski.
Sparse light snowfall accumulations up to a half-inch were observed 1-mile north-northeast of Sparks and 1 mile northeast of Carson City. No large impacts were noted.
Trained Weather Spotter 1 mile west of Doyle recorded 8 inches of snowfall in a 24 hour period.

Light to moderate snowfall accumulations were noted through the morning of the 25th across the Lake Tahoe Area with 7 inches of snow reported at Alpine Meadows Ski, 5 inches reported near Donner Summit, and 1 inch reported at the Truckee-Tahoe Airport. Residual snow showers occurred along the western portion of the Lake Tahoe Basin into the morning of the 26th. Alpine Meadows Ski reported 11 inches of snowfall and Homewood Ski reported 7 inches of snowfall over the 2-day period.
Mammoth Mountain Ski Resort reported 6 to 7 inches of snowfall overnight from the 24th into the morning of the 25th.
Over the Basin and Range of western Nevada, 4.5 inches of snow fell at Fernley with 3.6 inches falling at Lovelock. Slow going road travel was the main impact.

Moderate to heavy snowfall was reported across much of the area into the night of the 25th with areas in the North Valleys of Reno measuring 3 to 6.5 inches of snowfall, up to 5 inches in northern Reno, with 4.5 to 6 inches noted across Sparks and Spanish Springs, 2.5 inches in western Reno, 5 to 6.2 inches in south Reno, and up to 10 inches along the southwestern portion of the Carson Valley due to a lake-effect snow band the evening of the 26th. A slow-going commute with delays occurred for many areas.
Trained Weather Spotter 2 miles south-southeast of Sheridan reported 7.5 inches of lake-effect snowfall during the evening of the 25th.

Along the eastern portion of the Lake Tahoe Basin, 7 inches of snow fell at Heavenly Ski Resort, 6 inches a Diamond Peak Ski Area, and 6 inches at Mount Rose Ski Area. Some lake enhancement likely occurred over the southeastern shore, which contributed to the higher snowfall amount at Heavenly Ski Resort.

Multiple avalanches occurred in Walker Canyon with up to 15 feet of debris covering US 395. A snow plow was hit shortly after midnight the 28th and pushed into the Walker River. Fortunately, the driver was not killed but was hospitalized. Extreme avalanche danger was noted at the time from the Eastern Sierra Avalanche Center.

Very heavy snowfall was reported across the Greater Lake Tahoe Area with storm total snowfall totals of 2 to 5 feet above 7000 feet in the Lake Tahoe Basin with 12 to 30 inches at lake level. CA 89 was closed near Emerald Bay due to heavy snow and avalanche danger starting the 27th. Wind gusts were strong at times with gusts 45-50 mph. Sierra ridge gusts were as strong as 125 mph. California Highway Patrol also noted that Interstate 80 was closed between Colfax and the Nevada state line due to multiple spinouts for a period during the event.

Up to 76 inches of snowfall was reported at Mammoth Mountain. Snow totals across Mono County were generally 3 to 6 feet. US 395 was closed from Bishop to the Nevada State Line due to blizzard conditions and avalanche danger for the duration of the event. CA 203 was briefly closed near Mammoth Lakes the morning of the 27th. June Mountain ski area closed due to blizzard conditions. Wind gusts were strong at times with gusts to 45 to 50 mph. Sierra ridge gusts near Mammoth Mountain were as high as 80 mph.

Heavy snowfall was noted across much of northeastern California with Portola receiving 28 inches of snowfall, 18 inches of snowfall near Susanville, 13 inches of snowfall at Doyle, and 12 inches of snow in Janesville.

In the Lake Tahoe Basin, snow totals were 2 to 4 feet above 7000 feet with 12 to 30 inches at lake level. Strong winds were noted especially along the northern part of the Carson Range with Slide Mountain seeing gusts over 70 mph.

Snowfall varied from little to no valley accumulation due to mixing with rain to as much as 2 to 12 inches, with the highest totals occurring in southwest Reno and in Gardnerville, where as much as 18 to 24 inches of snow fell. Truckee Meadows Community College, Washoe County, and Carson City school districts were closed the 27th. COVID-19 vaccine clinics were closed in Virginia City. There were also power outages reported across Reno and Carson City, mainly on the 27th.

Widespread wind gusts between 50 to 60 MPH along the lower elevations of US 395 in the eastern Sierra, with several wind-prone areas seeing peak gusts greater than 60 MPH. Notable high gusts were 67 MPH at Conway Summit, 73 MPH at the head of Lundy Canyon, 103 MPH atop Mammoth Mountain, and 60 MPH near Toms Place.

Nevada 359 closed due to flooding and debris from CA-NV border to 18 miles into Nevada.
